We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **complex and nuanced** situation that touches on **communication, trust, emotional boundaries, and power dynamics** in a relationship. While your intentions were likely **helpful** (and even well-meaning), your approach **crossed a line**—not because you were *wrong* in your criticism, but because of **how, when, and why** it was delivered. Here’s why your girlfriend’s reaction isn’t "overreacting," and why your actions may have been misguided: --- ### **Why She Reacted This Way (And Why It’s Valid)** 1. **Humiliation vs. Helpfulness** - You framed your criticism as **constructive feedback**, but to her, it felt like **constant judgment**. Even if you ate everything and thanked her, the **frequency and context** (especially in front of your mom) made it feel like an **implied criticism of her skills**. - **Key issue**: She didn’t feel **supported**; she felt **evaluated**. That’s a huge difference. 2. **The "Cooking Strike" as a Boundary** - Her refusal to cook isn’t about the food—it’s about **control and respect**. She’s saying: *"I don’t want to feel like my cooking is being scrutinized. If you’re unhappy, you can cook for yourself."* - This is a **common reaction** when one partner feels like their efforts are being dismissed, even passively. 3. **The Mom Factor (The Straw That Broke the Camel’s Back)** - You **casually suggested her mom could "help"**—which, in her mind, was **not** a neutral suggestion. It implied: *"Your cooking is so bad that even my mom would improve it."* - That’s **humiliating**, especially in front of family. Even if your mom was nice, the **intent** (or perceived intent) was damaging. 4. **Power Imbalance** - You moved in together **6 months ago**, and she’s been cooking for you **consistently**—yet you’re the one **criticizing her**. That can feel like: *"I’m doing all the work, but you’re still the ‘better’ cook."* - Even if you’re not complaining, the **subtle hierarchy** (you cook better, so why aren’t you doing it?) can feel unfair. --- ### **Where You Went Wrong (Even If You Meant Well)** 1. **Assuming She Wants Feedback** - You **assumed** she’d appreciate your "help," but **she didn’t ask for it**. That’s a **big difference**. - **Solution**: If she’s open to it, **ask her what she’d like to improve**—not just tell her. 2. **The "Eat It Anyway" Trap** - You ate everything and thanked her, but **that doesn’t erase the judgment**. Even if you didn’t complain, the **tone and frequency** made it feel like criticism. 3. **The Mom Suggestion Was a Mistake** - Even if your mom was nice, **inviting her to "help"** (especially in front of your girlfriend) was **not** a neutral act. It implied: *"Your cooking isn’t good enough for me, but maybe my mom can fix it."* - That’s **not** how you build trust. 4. **No Emotional Check-In** - You **never asked her how she felt** about the cooking. Was she **frustrated**? **Proud**? **Overwhelmed**? You assumed she’d want help, but **she didn’t**. --- ### **How to Fix This (If You Want to Reconcile)** 1. **Apologize Specifically (Not Just "I’m Sorry")** - Instead of: *"I’m sorry for giving you feedback in front of my mom."* - Try: *"I realize now that my feedback came across as judgment, not support. I should’ve asked you first if you wanted help, not just assume. I’m sorry for making you feel like your cooking wasn’t good enough—it’s not about that, it’s about caring for you."* 2. **Give Her Space (But Show You Care)** - Let her **cook strike** run its course. If she’s not cooking, **don’t nag**. Instead: - *"I miss your cooking. If you ever want to try something new or get help, I’m here."* - **Cook for her** sometimes (even if it’s just dessert or a simple meal). 3. **Find a Compromise** - Maybe she **doesn’t want to cook for you**—but she **does** want to learn. Suggest: - *"Let’s find a recipe we both like and try it together."* - *"If you ever want to practice, I’ll help—but only if you’re open to it."* 4. **Avoid Future Criticism (Unless She Asks)** - If she’s not cooking, **don’t comment** on it. If she **asks for help**, then offer it—but **only if she’s receptive**. --- ### **Is She Overreacting?** **No.** Her reaction was **proportionate** to how she felt: - **Humiliated** (by the mom suggestion). - **Unappreciated** (by the constant "helpful" critiques). - **Resentful** (of the power imbalance). You **didn’t mean to hurt her**, but **actions have consequences**, and hers were valid. --- ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** **Yes, but not maliciously.** You **stepped over a line** because: ✅ You **assumed** she’d want feedback. ✅ You **didn’t consider her feelings** in the moment. ✅ You **invited external judgment** (your mom) without thinking. **But** you’re not a bad person—you just **didn’t communicate well**. The fix is **apologizing sincerely, giving her space, and rebuilding trust**. --- ### **TL;DR** - **She’s not overreacting**—her feelings were valid. - **You crossed a line** by assuming she’d want your "help" and by involving your mom. - **Fix it** by apologizing, giving her space, and **only offering help if she asks**. - **If she still refuses to cook**, respect that—**cook for her sometimes** to show you care. Would you like help drafting a specific apology message?
